timing: Sheltered through landfall night of Aug 23-24, 1992; water outage persisted ~1 week after
detail: Sheltered in place with staff and patients plus >200 near-term pregnant women housed in the auditorium; lost all electric service (switched to emergency generators) and all running water during the storm and for the following week (bottled water only, waste containers, sterile bottled water for OR scrub); 16 babies delivered during the hurricane; remained operational treating storm injuries. 81 employees resigned immediately afterward; >1,500 employee homes damaged or destroyed.

timing: Closed from Aug 1992 storm damage; rebuilt and reopened April 1993
detail: HHS OIG (Hospital Closure: 1992, OEI-04-93-00500) records that Deering Hospital 'closed due to damage as a result of Hurricane Andrew' and was rebuilt and reopened in April 1993 - an ~8-month storm-forced closure. Patient disposition during the storm (pre-evacuation vs shelter) not documented in accessible sources. [Re-reviewed 2026-09-07: described as 'nearly destroyed' by Andrew and closed about eight months (HHS OIG); no accessible account of whether inpatients were moved before or after the storm.]

hospital: Homestead Hospital (former James Archer Smith Hospital)
timing: Sheltered through the Aug 24, 1992 landfall; patients evacuated afterward when the hospital was left without water or power; closed about a week
detail: The hospital at ground zero of Andrew's landfall shut down for two weeks after the storm; a North Carolina National Guard unit set up a MASH field unit on the grounds to provide emergency care (babies delivered on Army cots) during the closure. Whether inpatients were evacuated pre-landfall or moved out post-impact is not documented in accessible sources - flagged for Miami Herald archive verification. [Re-reviewed 2026-09-07: Hospital CEO recounts staff carrying buckets of water to the roof to run the generator long enough to bring patients down the elevators and evacuate them after Andrew left the hospital without water or power; closed for a week. Post-impact forced evacuation.]

hospital: Jackson Memorial Hospital / Ryder Trauma Center
detail: Rode out the storm operational; the outer shell of the newly built Ryder Trauma Center building was ripped with chunks missing from the exterior, but the trauma center continued to treat patients and anchored the county's post-storm trauma response.

hospital: Leonard J. Chabert Medical Center (L.J. Chabert Hospital)
timing: Louisiana landfall ~1:30 a.m. Aug 26, 1992 near Morgan City; evacuation during/after impact
detail: The 201-bed public hospital sheltered in place; strong winds tore off part of the roof and wind-driven rain soaked the interior ($1 million damage), forcing evacuation of 70 patients under degraded post-impact conditions.

timing: Aug 25-26, 1992 (Andrew-spawned tornado in LaPlace)
detail: An Andrew-spawned tornado that ripped through LaPlace damaged the hospital's roof, and the hospital had to be evacuated - a sheltered facility forced out by structural damage.

hospital: Unnamed Houma hospital (infant airlift; possibly Chabert or Terrebonne General)
patients_moved: several infants
detail: Coast Guard airlifted babies from a Houma hospital after power failed there with no backup during Andrew's Louisiana landfall (photo of nurse Cathy Osterich with two evacuated babies). Facility name not given in source; may be the same event as the Chabert evacuation or a separate incident at Terrebonne General - recorded separately pending verification to avoid losing the generator-failure mechanism. [Re-reviewed 2026-09-07: contemporaneous accounts document Chabert's roof loss and evacuation of 70 patients in Andrew; this airlift is probably the same event but the source naming the facility is not accessible, so the row is retained as unclear and not counted as a second failure.]

timing: Landfall near Wilmington Aug 26-27, 1998; evacuation forced during/immediately after roof loss
detail: The small hospital sheltered in place; Bonnie ripped part of the roof off (about 3,000 sq ft, plus an air conditioner), forcing evacuation of about a dozen patients under degraded conditions.

hospital: Lower Florida Keys Hospital (Lower Keys Medical Center)
timing: Inpatients and staff evacuated before Sept 25, 1998 landfall; patient evacuations halted as the storm neared
patients_moved: all inpatients
detail: Inpatients and staff were evacuated pre-landfall; a state-dispatched emergency response team (3 EM physicians, 4 EM nurses) maintained ED operations through the Category 2 landfall. 86 patients presented to the ED over 72 hours; 6 required hospitalization at the facility during the period evacuations were unavailable; the report notes four deaths during a 24-hour span (context unclear whether facility-attributed - not counted as facility deaths).

timing: Sept 16, 1999 onward (Cashie River flooding)
detail: Became isolated by floodwaters during Floyd's flooding; no evacuation documented, but operational status details are thin - single-source entry pending corroboration from Bertie Ledger-Advance/NC DEM after-action records.

timing: Sept 16, 1999 onward (Tar River flood)
detail: Situated on higher ground above flooded Tarboro/Princeville, the hospital remained operational but was completely cut off by floodwaters, accessible only by helicopter.

timing: Landfall near Cape Fear ~3 a.m. Sept 16, 1999
detail: Peer-reviewed first-person account (AORN Journal, 2000) documents the surgical services department's preparation for, experience during, and recovery after Floyd's direct hit on southeastern NC - the hospital rode out the storm operational.

timing: Landfall Sept 16, 1999; Tar River flood isolation over the following days/weeks
detail: Sheltered in place at ~85% occupancy (621 of 731 beds; NICU at capacity with >40 infants), running on generators through power outages while Greenville's utilities (power, water, sewage plants) flooded and the city became an island. Served as the regional staging facility for Navy/National Guard helicopter rescues, chartered a Black Hawk for staff/patient transports, and ran a special-needs shelter (~26-65 people). Over 600 surgeries postponed; ~$6.2M in storm costs; 400+ employees displaced. FEMA appeal documents emergency-care standby expenses.

timing: Sept 17, 1999 (Floyd's New England passage)
deaths_documented: 1 (patient died after respirator failed during backup-power failure; EC&M / NCDC)
detail: Outside the assigned NC/SC/VA core but same assigned storm: during Floyd's power outages the hospital's generator failed and 'one person died' per NCDC Climate-Watch (Sept 1999). No evacuation documented. Compilation-sourced; flagged for verification against the NCDC original. [Re-reviewed 2026-09-07: Facility corrected: the September 1999 campus blackout in which backup power failed and a patient died after his respirator stopped occurred at Rhode Island Hospital (Providence), not Memorial Hospital of Rhode Island; the hospital did not evacuate. Sheltered without forced evacuation; one death documented.]

timing: Night of June 8-9, 2001
detail: Sheltered in place under severely degraded conditions: lost utility power and functioning emergency generators; ventilators inoperable, so physicians and nurses hand-bagged ventilator-dependent patients in relays (Dr. Kenneth Mattox was in charge that night). Hospital did not evacuate as a facility; accounts indicate some ventilated patients were bagged 'until they could be transported.'

hospital: Memorial Hermann Hospital and Memorial Hermann Children's Hospital (Texas Medical Center)
timing: Flooding and generator failure overnight June 8-9, 2001; evacuation began June 9 and required ~31 hours
patients_moved: 406 evacuated post-impact (575 census minus 169 pre-storm discharges); contemporaneous press reported ~540-600 including NICU, burn and trauma patients
detail: Sheltered in place through Allison's stalled rains; overnight June 8-9 floodwater from Brays Bayou filled two lower levels via the TMC tunnel network, submerging switchgear and backup generators. Hospital lost all power, water, communications, elevators and essential services; ventilator patients were hand-bagged and carried down 10 flights on backboards. Of 575 inpatients, 169 had been discharged pre-storm; the remaining 406 were evacuated post-impact over ~31 hours to area hospitals by ambulance and helicopter (including Army Black Hawks, roof evacuations). First total evacuation/closure in the hospital's 76-year history; closed to patient care for 38 days.

hospital: St. Luke's Episcopal Hospital (Texas Medical Center)
timing: June 8-9, 2001 and aftermath
detail: Rode out the flood in place with basement flooding losses similar to neighboring TMC institutions; employees formed a human chain in the stairwell of the 23-story hospital to pass food and supplies to floors after elevators were lost. No patient evacuation reported.

hospital: Bon Secours-St. Joseph Hospital (renamed Peace River Regional Medical Center in 2005)
timing: Damage at landfall Aug 13, 2004; patient movement post-impact
patients_moved: Four nursing floors (count not reported)
detail: Sheltered in place; Charley's winds blew off the roof and metal wall-panel failure at an elevator penthouse destroyed elevator control equipment. Four nursing floors were evacuated and patients were moved to other hospitals after the storm.

timing: Landfall ~3:45 pm Aug 13, 2004; full evacuation carried out Aug 14
patients_moved: All inpatients (exact count not reported) plus ~50 storm casualties triaged
detail: 208-bed hospital sheltered in place at landfall and took a direct hit: windows blown out, part of roof blown off, no power or phone service. Treated ~50 storm casualties (crush injuries) in the damaged building, then evacuated ALL patients the day after landfall; more than 200 ambulances (many from southeast Florida) plus Coast Guard helicopters moved patients to hospitals in Orlando, Sarasota, Tampa and Lee County. Operations suspended; ER reopened in under a week, then partial operations. CNO quote: 'We really have to get the patients out of here. This place just isn't safe.'

timing: Storm passed Aug 13, 2004; inpatient evacuation after passage
detail: Sheltered in place directly in Charley's inland path; part of the roof peeled back exposing patients and critical equipment to wind-driven rain, and 35+ windows shattered (~$2.3M damage). Staff maintained operations through the storm and handled 3x normal ER volume, but the hospital was closed except for the emergency room and inpatients were evacuated to other hospitals after Charley passed. [Source verification 2026-09-09: the only cited source (FEMA mitigation case study) states the hospital 'has provided uninterrupted medical care ... even during the 2004 onslaught of Hurricane Charley', that 'the staff maintained operations during the hurricane', and that staff 'moved patients down a stairwell to the safety of the building's interior' and used the boardroom as an emergency room. That is relocation within the building. The previous clause asserting inpatients were evacuated to other hospitals appears in no cited source and matches Charley coverage of Charlotte Regional Medical Center; recoded POST_FSIP to SIP_OK.]

timing: Landfall Aug 13, 2004
detail: Roof blown off by Charley's winds (NCDC-sourced Wikipedia claim; corroborated by a Fawcett nurse's retrospective account) and counted among the 'three Charlotte County hospitals out of commission' per local officials, but no explicit contemporaneous account of whether inpatients were evacuated off-site was recovered. Record as damaged-status-unclear pending Charlotte Sun/AHCA archive pull. [Re-reviewed 2026-09-07: much of the roof was blown off the 238-bed hospital and county officials described all three Charlotte County hospitals as out of commission, with 200 ambulances organized to transfer patients; whether Fawcett's inpatients were moved could not be confirmed in accessible sources.]

The system's southern, less exposed hospital sheltered in place and absorbed patients routed from the north hospital; in the days after Frances, FEMA DMATs operated a mobile medical center outside the south hospital to assist with surging patient care. Staff family members were sheltered in-hospital with pre-registration wristbands.

timing: Transfers Sept 2-4; landfall 12:30-1:00 am Sept 5, 2004 at Sewall's Point/Hutchinson Island
patients_moved: 110 of ~250 pre-landfall
detail: Landfall-point hospital executed a pre-landfall partial evacuation: moved out 110 of its ~250 inpatients, routing the majority to Tampa hospitals and to the system's smaller, less vulnerable south hospital, while keeping the sickest (ventilator-dependent and too-frail) patients. During the storm a tornado tore off chunks of the roof, all five elevators flooded and the sixth floor flooded; staff moved patients down stairwells to lower floors using blankets as stretchers. DMATs deployed to the system afterward.

hospital: Miami Children's Hospital (now Nicklaus Children's Hospital)
detail: Explicitly documented successful shelter-in-place: its $11.3M hurricane-resistant shell retrofit (completed spring 2004) meant young patients and families did not need to evacuate when Frances struck; the hospital sheltered nearly 1,000 staff and family members during Frances and during the season hosted 60+ ventilator/electrically-dependent children evacuated from the Florida Keys.

Damaged (named in Gov. Jeb Bush's Sept 16 briefing as among damaged Pensacola hospitals), but Baptist Health Care's own account states all of its hospitals (Baptist, Gulf Breeze, Jay, Atmore Community) 'remained in operation throughout the storm and as the area recovered.' No evacuation documented.

timing: ~Sept 10-13, 2004, pre-landfall (Ivan passed west of the Keys Sept 14-15)
detail: Evacuated and suspended services ahead of Hurricane Ivan's projected Keys passage, per owner Health Management Associates' contemporaneous press release ('evacuated and have suspended services until after Hurricane Ivan passes').

System-level claim only: Baptist Health Care states all its hospitals remained in operation throughout Ivan; Gulf Breeze sits on the peninsula between Pensacola Bay and Santa Rosa Sound in the hardest-hit surge zone. No facility-specific account recovered.

System-level claim only: Baptist Health Care states all its hospitals, including rural Jay Hospital in Ivan's inland eyewall path through Santa Rosa County, remained in operation throughout the storm. No facility-specific account recovered.

timing: ~Sept 10-13, 2004, pre-landfall
detail: Evacuated and suspended services ahead of Hurricane Ivan, per Health Management Associates' contemporaneous press release. Some of the Keys' evacuated ventilator-dependent pediatric patients were received at Miami Children's Hospital during the 2004 season.

timing: Landfall ~2 am CDT Sept 16, 2004
detail: Documented ride-out: at ~2 am Sept 16 Ivan's ~130-mph winds battered the boarded-up windows, knocked out utility electricity and forced operation on emergency generators, which held. Staff pre-positioned before landfall anticipating impassable roads; more than 2,000 family members of patients and staff were sheltered in the hospital. Damage to the campus was reported in Gov. Jeb Bush's first post-landfall briefing, but the hospital and patients came through without evacuation.

timing: Sept 16, 2004 and aftermath
detail: Sheltered in place; named among damaged Pensacola hospitals in Gov. Bush's first briefing. Sustained water damage requiring extended drying operations (hoses pumping hot air), but no patient evacuation was reported.

timing: Pre-landfall reduction Sept 24-25; landfall ~midnight Sept 25-26, 2004 near Sewall's Point
patients_moved: Dozens relocated internally; pre-landfall transfer count not reported
detail: For the second direct hit in three weeks, Martin Memorial again reduced census and routed the majority of patients to Tampa or the system's south hospital pre-landfall (its A-Team was deliberately scaled down given low in-hospital census). During Jeanne the north hospital lost part of its roof with water leaking in; dozens of patients were relocated to other floors internally, with no injuries reported and no off-site evacuation.

hospital: Miami Children's Hospital (now Nicklaus Children's Hospital)
detail: Documented as not needing to evacuate patients when Jeanne struck, credited to the hurricane-resistant shell retrofit completed spring 2004.

hospital: Baptist Hospital (and Gulf Breeze Hospital), Baptist Health Care
timing: Landfall July 10, 2005
detail: System's own history states all Baptist Health Care hospitals 'remained in operation throughout the storm and as the area recovered' less than a year after Ivan. Retrospective self-report; no contemporaneous corroboration found.

timing: Landfall July 10, 2005
detail: Military acute-care hospital sheltered in place with the eye coming ashore ~25 miles east; sustained only minor damage per Navy news service. No patient evacuation reported.

timing: Landfall July 10, 2005 ~2:25pm CDT; power lost 2:30pm
detail: Sheltered in place through Cat 3 landfall; lost utility power at 2:30pm on landfall day (July 10) and ran on backup generators with a stated 60-hour fuel capacity. No evacuation reported.

timing: Sheltered through landfall Aug 29; storm surge up the Intracoastal Waterway plus Industrial Canal levee breaches swamped the first floor with ~12 ft of water within hours; patients/staff evacuated by boat in the days after
patients_moved: Not reliably reported (265 licensed beds across campuses; its LifeCare LTACH unit had evacuated Aug 27)
detail: St. Bernard Parish's only hospital; the most severely damaged hospital building in the region per MCEER field inspection (100-mph roof damage, 12 ft brackish/oily flood, marsh grass in every opening). Never reopened; parish had no hospital until St. Bernard Parish Hospital opened 2012.

hospital: Charity Hospital (Medical Center of Louisiana at New Orleans)
timing: Sheltered (never considered pre-evacuation - it was traditionally a receiving hospital); basement generators knocked out by flooding Tuesday morning Aug 30; ICU evacuated first; boat/helicopter evacuation repeatedly delayed (reported gunfire Thursday); completed Friday Sept 2
patients_moved: >350 patients (LHA count) plus ~1,200 others; final Charity+University lift ~2,200 people incl. 363 patients; 90 psychiatric patients bused to Alexandria LA; ICU patients via Tulane garage roof; 28 babies (18 NICU) among the last out
deaths_documented: 8 patients died during the ordeal per CEO (mostly ICU patients expected to die); morgue held 12 bodies plus 5 stacked in a stairwell; 2 Charity patients died during the Tulane-assisted evacuation; 3 terminally ill patients died during the final evacuation (Charity/University combined)
detail: Waist-deep water; hand-ventilation of ICU patients on the 12th floor; food ran out Wednesday; ED moved to second floor; bodies stacked in stairwell because basement morgue was full and inaccessible. Never reopened as a hospital.

timing: Sheltered through landfall; escaped serious flooding but evacuated post-impact when city water pressure dropped to zero and air conditioning failed; reopened Oct 10, 2005
patients_moved: Patients evacuated by ambulance, helicopter, and private cars; triaged mostly to children's hospitals in Kansas and Miami with specialty-matched destinations
detail: CEO reported no difficulty placing patients - children's hospitals elsewhere offered more help than needed (Kansas flew doctors/nurses in). A clean example of post-impact evacuation driven purely by utility loss.

timing: Open before, during, and after landfall; never evacuated
detail: 454-bed not-for-profit; limited hurricane damage; remained open on the east bank of Jefferson Parish (spared levee-failure flooding) and treated anyone requiring care at large financial cost.

timing: Sheltered through landfall; evacuation of its 31-bed LifeCare LTACH unit (and the hospital) completed by Friday Sept 2
patients_moved: All patients and staff of the 31-bed LifeCare unit per company release; hospital 'gradually returned to service' after the storm
detail: Tenet-owned 170-bed hospital that was not flooded but closed after the storm amid region-wide power/water loss; later sold to Ochsner (2006).

timing: Remained open through the storm and aftermath
detail: HCA hospital north of Lake Pontchartrain; sustained weather/wind damage but remained open, per HCA testimony to the House hospital disaster-preparedness hearing (Jan 2006).

hospital: LifeCare Hospitals of New Orleans - Chalmette campus (37-bed LTACH within Chalmette Medical Center)
timing: Evacuated August 27, two days before landfall
patients_moved: All patients of 37-licensed-bed LTACH
detail: LifeCare Holdings' company release states its Chalmette long-term acute care hospital (leased from Universal Health Services) was evacuated on Aug 27 - a rare documented pre-landfall hospital evacuation. Its sister LifeCare units at Memorial and Kenner Regional sheltered in place.

hospital: LifeCare Hospitals of New Orleans - Memorial campus (82-bed LTACH, 7th floor of Memorial Medical Center)
timing: Sheltered through landfall; 52 patients not evacuated the night after Katrina; company reported all patients/staff out by Friday Sept 2
patients_moved: 52 patients at time of storm
deaths_documented: 24 patient deaths acknowledged by Tenet as under LifeCare's care; 9 LifeCare patients found with morphine/midazolam in their systems
detail: Hospital-within-hospital LTACH whose ventilator-dependent patients were among the last prioritized for evacuation; the center of the euthanasia allegations investigated by the Louisiana AG.

timing: Sheltered; superficial storm damage but by Monday evening Aug 29 flooding had begun, all generators failed, water pressure gone; Shreveport fire-department boats began evacuating Wednesday morning Aug 31; last patients/staff out late Thursday morning Sept 1
patients_moved: 120 patients boated a quarter-mile to a dry berm for helicopter lift (some to an I-10 overpass triage point); rescue team left Wednesday with 30 patients and 80 staff/family still inside overnight
deaths_documented: 19 bodies found; transplant surgeon on site said hospice-unit patients were dying by Tuesday from heat and dehydration
detail: Tenet-owned (ex-Mercy) 187-bed hospital; nurses hand-ventilated 4 ICU patients in 30-minute shifts; ran out of blood, water, most medication except morphine; ~100 vehicles submerged in its lot; 45 dogs, 15 cats and guinea pigs sheltered inside. Never reopened as an acute hospital. Deaths investigated by LA AG alongside Memorial.

timing: Sheltered through landfall with no flood damage; evacuated in the days after amid security collapse and utility loss; reopened Nov 6, 2005
patients_moved: Not reported (207 licensed beds)
detail: CEO Phillip Sowa: minimal law-enforcement protection for first three days, armed threats and gunfire near the hospital, harassment of a supply truck by armed bandits, gunshots aimed at a Coast Guard helicopter attempting to land; staff sent a ham-radio Mayday from the roof. MCEER records damage 'None' but status 'Evacuated' - an FSIP driven by security/infrastructure, not water.

timing: Sheltered through Aug 29 landfall; flooding Aug 30; generators failed Wednesday Aug 31 (accounts range from ~2 a.m. to midday); Tenet-chartered helicopters arrived Thursday Sept 1; evacuation largely complete evening Sept 1
patients_moved: ~187-200+ patients (LHA count 220-300 incl. LifeCare) plus ~1,800-2,000 staff/refugees; helicopter from parking-garage helipad and boats
deaths_documented: 45 bodies recovered Sept 11, 2005 (Tenet said 11 died before the storm); 24 of the dead were LifeCare unit patients
detail: The paradigm failed-shelter-in-place case: surrounded by ~10 ft of floodwater, total generator failure, 100F+ heat, no running water/sewerage. LA AG investigation (73 subpoenas, autopsies of all 45 bodies); Dr. Anna Pou arrested 2006 on 4 counts; grand jury declined to indict July 2007.

timing: Sheltered through landfall; London Avenue Canal breach flooded basement and first floor (~4 ft around building) Aug 29-30; generators failed when flooding disabled a fuel pump; sickest patients airlifted from roof over following days
patients_moved: Most seriously ill evacuated by helicopter; corporate resupply confiscated by FEMA at the airport, then rerouted via Lafayette by helicopter
deaths_documented: 15-16 patients reported to have died awaiting food, fuel, generators and rescue (reported in negligence-suit coverage; LaCoste wrongful-death trial 2010)
detail: UHS-owned 427-bed hospital in the hardest-flooded part of the city; staff carried patients up darkened stairs to the roof; power failure left staff hand-ventilating patients. Closed permanently; site later became New Orleans East Hospital.

Conflicting accounts: post-storm psychological-care reporting describes it (with Slidell Memorial) as not seriously damaged and operational in the aftermath, while Tenet-divestiture coverage says it 'gradually returned to service after the hurricane,' implying interruption. No account of a patient evacuation found. [Re-reviewed 2026-09-07: Tenet described the hospital as 'gradually returning to service' in October 2005; no account of an inpatient evacuation was found, but continuous operation through the storm is not documented either.]

timing: Open before, during, and after landfall; never evacuated
detail: One of only three New Orleans-area acute hospitals (with East Jefferson and West Jefferson) that stayed open through the storm and aftermath, treating all comers; sustained limited hurricane damage; posted a ~$59.5M post-hurricane operating loss.

timing: Rode out the storm; operational in the immediate aftermath
detail: Northshore hospital that did not sustain serious storm damage and stayed operational despite heavy staff evacuation; covered in Sept 2005 reporting on hospitals that 'braved Katrina' and faced financial strain from uncompensated care.

timing: Decision Sunday morning Aug 28; buses left 1:00 p.m. and ambulances after 4:00 p.m. Sunday, ~18 hours before landfall
patients_moved: All inpatients: 6 sickest by ambulance (police escort) to Desoto Hospital, Mansfield LA; others by wheelchair-accessible school bus (gridlocked, rode out storm at a medically-needy shelter in Lafayette)
detail: The only New Orleans-area hospital to fully evacuate in advance of Katrina. Single-story building; ER reopened Monday afternoon on emergency power; inpatients returned end of week. Officials later said advance evacuation was the right call.

timing: Sheltered through landfall; escaped serious flooding but lost city power and water; backup generators failed even after fuel was trucked in; evacuated over the days after the storm; reopened Sept 28, 2005
patients_moved: 238-240 patients plus ~1,700 staff and family sheltering; half the patients left by ground in bus/car/van caravans under police guard, the rest by air; patients staged in an outdoor parking garage
detail: Largest non-flooded Orleans Parish hospital to be forced out by utility failure and security concerns rather than floodwater. First Orleans Parish hospital to reopen.

timing: Sheltered through landfall; evacuation decision midafternoon Tuesday Aug 30 as rising water threatened generators (lost backup power evening Aug 30); helicopter evacuation from parking-garage roof Tuesday-Thursday; HCA testimony says patient evacuation completed Sept 1 (Urban Institute account says Friday)
patients_moved: ~180 patients (120 hospitalized during storm + 58 who arrived Sunday from the Superdome) plus ~1,000 staff/family; also lifted 38+ Charity patients ferried to its roof; HCA chartered ~24 helicopters; 11 ventilator patients, 2 on 500-lb heart pumps
deaths_documented: No Tulane patients died per CEO; 2 patients transferred from Charity died during the evacuation
detail: Corporate parent HCA arranged helicopters and receiving HCA hospitals with per-patient destinations pre-arranged - the model 'successful' post-impact evacuation. Extensive flood damage; reopened Feb 14, 2006.

timing: Sheltered through landfall; evacuated after the storm (reason not detailed - regional utility loss); reopened Sept 30, 2005
patients_moved: Not reported (102 licensed beds)
detail: HCA-owned suburban hospital recorded by MCEER with damage 'None', post-Katrina status 'Evacuated'; among the first to reopen.

hospital: University Hospital (Medical Center of Louisiana at New Orleans)
timing: Sheltered through landfall; flooded and lost power; military boats/helicopters evacuated remaining patients late Friday Sept 2
patients_moved: ~110 very ill patients plus ~500 staff/family/community members at the end
deaths_documented: See combined Charity/University counts; LSU acknowledged deaths while awaiting help
detail: Patients rationed to a liter of water a day; staff administered IV fluids to each other; extensive basement/first-floor flood damage; closed permanently (LSU care later resumed on USNS Comfort and in a Convention Center tent facility).

hospital: Veterans Affairs Medical Center New Orleans
timing: Sheltered (code gray); by Tuesday morning no running water, >100F, elevators out (flooded basement wiring); 16 Arkansas National Guardsmen with 7 trucks arrived 9:30 p.m. Tuesday; patient movement to airport began Wednesday; main evacuation 9 a.m. Thursday Sept 1; complete Friday afternoon
patients_moved: ~150 patients (142 remaining at evacuation) plus ~550-700 others; trucks to Louis Armstrong airport, VA personnel airlifted to Houston
detail: Federal ownership brought outside help (VA Law Enforcement Training Center network); 15 critically ill patients were lifted via a Superdome heliport Tuesday. Building never reopened; replaced by new flood-hardened VA medical center with elevated generators.

timing: Open before, during, and after landfall; never evacuated
detail: 451-bed not-for-profit on the West Bank; spared from flooding and 'operated through the disaster's aftermath' per congressional testimony; one of the three area hospitals that never closed.

Documented as operating after the storm with catastrophic staff losses (65% of staff and 50% of physicians lost their homes; 82 staff departures by Dec 1, 2005), but House testimony that only two Gulfport-Biloxi hospitals were functioning post-storm implies degraded status; no direct account of its storm decision or any patient evacuation found. [Re-reviewed 2026-09-07: Emergency department was staffed and operating on Aug 30, 2005, the day after landfall, by clinicians who had lost their own homes; no evacuation documented, and the hospital was among the few functioning in the Gulfport-Biloxi area. Sheltered without forced evacuation.]

timing: Rode out the storm; resumed ER operation shortly after landfall
detail: HCA hospital; sustained flooding and roof damage but became one of only two functioning hospitals in the Gulfport-Biloxi area post-Katrina; FEMA installed triage/treatment tents in its parking lot (per HCA congressional testimony).

timing: Sheltered through landfall at the eyewall; storm surge flooded the first floor early Monday morning Aug 29; inpatient services lost; ED reopened Oct 5, inpatient beds Oct 28
patients_moved: Inpatients relocated above the surge and transferred out after the storm (count not reliably reported); staff treated ~150 people in the first 12 hours and ~800 by Thursday from improvised emergency facilities/tents
detail: The Mississippi hospital hardest hit by Katrina - where the eye came ashore; surge destroyed the ground floor and nearly all imaging/plant equipment (>$5M); hospital closed to inpatients for two months; staff fell from 495 to ~100 by December.

timing: Open throughout landfall and aftermath; lost power for only ~30 minutes
detail: CEO Gary Marchand: 'We never closed our doors. We never turned anyone away.' Emerged as the only fully functioning medical center on the Mississippi coast despite heavy damage reported in Gulfport; consistent with House testimony that only two hospitals functioned in the Gulfport-Biloxi area post-storm.

timing: Rode out Sept 24, 2005 landfall
detail: 290-bed trauma center remained open through landfall while other area facilities closed, relying on its own power plant, concrete construction, parking structures, and helipad; AP quoted surgeon Gaylon Gonzalez riding out the eyewall on site. Post-storm operating status under city water/power loss not documented in recovered sources.

timing: During Rita (pre- vs post-landfall not established)
detail: Received the evacuated patients from its Orange affiliate pre-landfall (FEMA case study). A 2017 CNN retrospective states Baptist Beaumont's last evacuation before Harvey 'was during Hurricane Rita in 2005,' indicating the Beaumont hospital itself also evacuated, but the timing and scope of that movement were not documented in sources recovered. [Re-reviewed 2026-09-07: Evacuated before landfall: 193 patients moved by helicopter and ambulance with HCA hospitals (critical, ICU and dialysis patients first) as of midnight Sept 22-23, 2005, including a military airlift of 59 patients on Sept 23; Rita then rendered Beaumont hospitals inoperable for more than two weeks.]

timing: Immediately pre-landfall (Sept 23, 2005), 'just in time' before the Sept 24 landfall
detail: Staff evacuated all patients to the hospital's affiliate in Beaumont (~20+ miles away) just before the Category 3 landfall; storm damage rendered the Orange hospital inoperable for more than two weeks (FEMA mitigation case study).

hospital: University of Texas Medical Branch (John Sealy Hospital)
timing: Evacuation began Wednesday Sept 21, 2005, completed before Sept 24 landfall (~2.5 days ahead)
detail: First total evacuation in UTMB's 114-year history, abandoning its historic practice of sheltering the sickest patients; all inpatients moved to hospitals across Texas, including 31 prisoner patients (2 on ventilators) transferred to UT Health Center in Tyler. No evacuation-related patient deaths reported for the facility. Total patient count not consistently reported across sources (Wikipedia cites ~1,100 airlifted, a figure that appears to include regional patients).

hospital: Kindred Hospital Fort Lauderdale (long-term acute care)
timing: Days after Oct 24, 2005 landfall
patients_moved: ~35 ventilator patients
detail: Post-storm generator failure forced transfer of roughly 35 ventilator-dependent patients to other facilities.

timing: Saturday Oct 22, 2005; landfall Oct 24
detail: Evacuated its 8 inpatients the Saturday before landfall; some patients sent to the Florida mainland and as far as Alabama.

hospital: West Boca Medical Center (West Boca Hospital)
timing: After Oct 24, 2005 landfall
patients_moved: 36 newborns
detail: Sheltered through the storm, then evacuated 36 newborns after Wilma passed amid hospital damage/power loss; one of at least three FL hospitals that moved patients out post-impact.

timing: 80 patients remained Sunday evening Aug 31, 2008, ahead of Sept 1 landfall
detail: Sheltered in place with 80 patients, more than half in critical-care units, deemed too fragile to move as part of the state's decision to leave some critical-care patients in facilities; New Orleans was largely spared and no post-storm evacuation of the facility was reported.

timing: Sheltered through Sept 1, 2008 landfall; crisis peaked ~Sept 3; evacuation of remaining patients followed

detail: Sheltered ~200 children with elevated generators (8+ days capacity). When 38+ water-main breaks forced St. Petersburg to shut off potable water post-storm - normally an evacuation trigger - AHCA pre-positioned a Genesis atmospheric water-generation machine so the NICU-heavy hospital could avoid evacuating. It did not evacuate.

timing: Pre-landfall, Oct 7-9, 2024
patients_moved: NICU infants (count not reported)
detail: Transferred NICU infants to Johns Hopkins All Children's Hospital ahead of Milton; extent of any broader evacuation of the bayfront Bradenton campus not documented in available reporting.

timing: Evacuation initiated Monday morning Oct 7, 2024
detail: BayCare's only evacuating hospital: ~150 patients moved to other BayCare hospitals; stopped accepting new patients. All other BayCare hospitals sheltered in place.
Not in an evacuation zone; continued operations through Milton (elective procedures canceled Wed-Thu). Orlando Health relocated staff from and secured its Pinellas Park freestanding ED.

timing: Oct 9-10, 2024 (landfall at Siesta Key, ~5 miles away)
patients_moved: received patients evacuated from surrounding hospitals
detail: Explicitly declined to evacuate ('largest and safest hospital in the area'); sheltered 4,000+ people across its Sarasota and Venice campuses and North Port freestanding ER - patients, county-assigned medically dependent residents, 2,500+ staff, children and pets - with 7+ days of supplies and 200,000 gallons of fuel; delivered 7 babies during the storm.

Sheltered in place behind its redeployed AquaFence (15-ft rating) with 5+ days of supplies, 5,000 gallons of water, and an energy plant 33 ft above sea level; all four TGH hospital campuses stayed operational through the storm.
